Fluoroscopic antero-posterior view in a 3-year-old female patient showing the position of the five electrodes (red arrows) implanted in the suboccipital region for the treatment of spastic diplegia. The electrodes were implanted in a single procedure over a guide wire (blue arrow). The first electrode was placed at the cervico-dorsal region close to the myelon and the last two electrodes were placed in the sacral region close to the filum terminale. The electrodes were placed 3-4 cm apart. The electrodes should be placed in the suboccipital region in order to evade the peripheral resistance and ensure the electrodes will place the majority of their electrical power in the central nervous system. The central electrodes are placed in the region of the dorsal spinal cord with the majority of the electrodes positioned dorsal to the spinal cord. The electrodes placed in the dorsal half of the spinal cord are most likely to evade the peripheral resistance. The electrodes placed in the ventral half of the spinal cord might be able to place their electrical power in the central nervous system. The electrodes placed in the lower half of the spinal cord should be positioned close to the filum terminale so that they will place their electrical power in the central nervous system. The patient has bilateral congenital hip dislocation (yellow arrows) and a congenital lumbar hernia (black arrow) that are not related to the spinal cord stimulation procedure.

Demonstration of the method used to measure the interincisal angle (the angle between the long axes of the teeth adjacent to the incisal edge), the angle of the upper incisors to the mandibular plane, and the angle of the mandibular plane to the midsagittal plane using panoramic radiograph measurements. Line A shows the long axis of the upper right canine, Line L1 shows the long axis of the upper right canine. Point a is the most anterior point on the root of the upper right canine. Line B shows the long axis of the upper right canine, Line L2 shows the long axis of the upper right canine. Point b is the intersection of Line A and Line L1. A 50-year-old male patient who had received a single-dose of TGA was admitted to our hospital with a severe head injury. He had an initial GCS of 15. After a subarachnoid hemorrhage was observed on computed tomography of the brain, he was admitted to ICU with a tube drainage system implanted. The patient suffered from severe hypotension and bradycardia for about 2 h after the operation. The patient's condition was observed to have deteriorated, and he was transferred to the ICU. We considered the possibility of cerebral infarction because he suffered from an acute episode of loss of consciousness and weakness of the right limbs. After emergent re-intubation, emergent cerebral angiography was performed. The angiography revealed a cerebral aneurysm in the anterior communicating artery (red arrow). We also observed a cerebral infarction of the right MCA territory.

Radiographic measurements. The center of each circle is the midpoint between the two points on each side of the growth plate. The two vertical lines perpendicular to each growth plate are drawn, and the angle between them is the tibiotalar joint line angle (JL). The horizontal distance from the midpoint of each growth plate to the point where the two vertical lines intersect the horizontal plane is the growth plate length (JL). The horizontal distance from the midpoint of the tibia to the point where the two vertical lines intersect the horizontal plane is the calcaneal specific angle (CS). The angle between the two vertical lines is the tibiotalar joint line angle (JL) (yellow lines) and is measured in the weight bearing plane. The vertical lines are drawn perpendicular to the growth plates and are marked at their intersection with the horizontal plane. These lines designate the calcaneal specific angle (CS) (red lines), measured between the calcaneal and the tibiotalar joint planes.

Definition of the six possible directions (white arrows) toward the scala tympani in the horizontal plane. The scala tympani is the inner ear structure located in the deepest part of the tympanic cavity and is defined by the scala tympani (white circle) and the tympanic membrane (transparent arrow). The possible directions are six lines drawn from the scala tympani toward the scala vestibuli. Two of the possible directions are perpendicular to the tympanic membrane (black arrows). The distances (short white arrows) between the scala tympani and each of the six possible directions were used to calculate the possible positions on the tympanic membrane where a sound would be transmitted most directly toward the scala tympani. The possible positions were defined as points on a circle whose radius was the distance between the scala tympani and the scala vestibuli, and whose center was the scala tympani.

The dentoalveolar region includes dentoalveolar space (asterisk) and areas with missing teeth. Additionally, the region includes the area around teeth with oro-/hypodontia, the area with missing teeth such as teeth with unerupted germs or congenitally missing teeth, and the edentulous space. The dentoalveolar region includes the area around teeth with missing teeth such as unerupted germs and congenitally missing teeth, as well as the edentulous space; however, in this example, the edentulous space is not visible on the image. The dentoalveolar area also includes the oro-/hypo-/atonia of the teeth. Finally, the area around teeth and the alveolar bone that are associated with oro-/hypo-dontia and/or atonia, such as missing teeth, unerupted germs, and other anomalies, is included in this region.

The method of measuring hyoid bone position. The most superior point of the hyoid bone (H) is marked on the midsagittal plane (MP) and the distance between the most superior point of the hyoid bone (H) and the most superior point of the clivus (C) is marked (T–H). The distance between these two points is transposed to the midsagittal plane (MP) and marked on the midsagittal plane (MP–H). The angle between the T–H line and the MP–H line is the angle of hyoid bone position

Disc height was measured 10 mm above the intervertebral disc space on the anterior endplate of the cranial vertebra and on the posterior endplate of the caudal vertebra. Disc height is calculated as the distance from the midpoint of the cranial endplate to the midpoint of the caudal endplate. Disc height was measured at the L1–2, L2–3, L3–4, and L4–5 intervertebral disc spaces. When the cranial endplate was not visible or the caudal endplate was not fully visible on the radiograph, the cranial or caudal endplate was used to measure the disc height, and the cranial and caudal endplates were used to measure the disc height.

Definition of the ED, FD distances and the D-line. The EDdistance is defined as the perpendicular distance between the antero-superior corner and the point at which the line DL intersects the antero-superior wall of the tympanic cavity. The FDdistance is defined as the perpendicular distance between the antero-superior corner and the point at which the line FL intersects the floor of the hypotympanic cavity. The D-line is drawn from the antero-superior corner to the point at which the line DL intersects the antero-superior wall of the tympanic cavity. The E-line is drawn from the antero-superior corner to the point at which the line FL intersects the floor of the hypotympanic cavity.

The width of the canal is measured as RM from the root apexes of the maxillary incisors, and the width of the canal is measured as RP from the root apexes of the maxillary canines. The width of the canal from the incisive foramen to the incisive canal is measured as Ca. The canal width is defined as the average of the distances between the canal and the palatal bone surfaces, and this average value is defined as the canal width.

Illustration of the method of measurement in the mid-sagittal plane during vaginal sonohysterography. The vaginal wall was segmented and colored by the vaginal sonography software. The boundaries of the vaginal lumen were traced by the sonographer in the first step. Subsequently the software automatically colored the vaginal wall. This illustration shows the measurement of the vaginal wall thickness (VWT) in a 72-year-old woman with a vaginal canal length of 11 cm. The VWT was 3.6 mm (red line). The VWT was determined at 1.5 cm away from the vaginal fornices (white lines). The horizontal orange line was constructed by subtracting the VWT from the vaginal canal length (11cm – 3.6mm = 7.4cm). The vaginal wall was segmented along this line. The red curved line is the zone of interest (ROI) where the color map was automatically created.

To define the anterior displacement, the longitudinal axis of the tibial component is drawn. The condylar angle (Ang) is the angle between the long axis of the condylar processes and the mandibular plane. It is measured by drawing a line from the center of the condylar head (R) to the gonial angle (M) on each side and measuring the angle between these two lines. An angle of 90 degrees between these two lines indicates a normal position of the condyle.

Example image of myocardial T2* measurement.Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) images were used to validate the T2* measurements in a sample of 50 consecutive short-axis slices from the end-diastolic frame of a single patient. All LGE‐free slices were manually segmented, and a 4‐slice overlap was created. In this example, the myocardium with signal loss (purple) was considered as tissue with LGE and therefore was assigned a T2* value of 0.89 s‐1. In the same patient, myocardial T2* values were recorded in LGE‐free neighboring slices from a second pass through the acquisition volume.
